paragraph: Methods & Meanings MEDIAN The mean is a useful way to determine the center when data values are close together or are evenly spaced. Another tool, the median, also locates the approximate ‘center’ of a set of data in a different way. The median is the middle number in a set of data arranged numerically. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle numbers. The median is more accurate than the mean as a way to describe the center when there are outliers in the data set. Suppose the following data set represents the number of home runs hit by the best seven players on a Major League Baseball team: 16, 26, 21, 9, 13, 15, and 9. In this example, the median is 15. This is because when the data are arranged in order (9, 9, 13, 15, 16, 21, 26), the middle number is 15. Mean and median are called measures of central tendency because they each describe the ‘center’ of a set of data, but in different ways.
gpt_oss_or_reasoning: The paragraph only explains concepts and provides an example; it does not present an error, compare student work, or warn about common mistakes.

Methods & Meanings: FRACTION DIVISION

Method 1: Using diagrams.
To divide by a fraction using a diagram, create a model of the situation using rectangles, a linear model, or a visual representation of it. Then break that model into the fractional parts named.
For example, to divide 7/8 ÷ 1/2, you can draw the diagram shown to visualize how many 1/2-sized pieces fit into 7/8. The diagram shows that one 1/2 fits once, with 3/8 of a whole remaining. Since 3/8 is 3/4 of 1/2, you can see that 1 3/4 half-sized pieces fit into 7/8, so 7/8 ÷ 1/2 = 1 3/4.

Method 2: Using common denominators.
To divide a number by a fraction using common denominators, express both numbers as fractions with the same denominator. Then divide the first numerator by the second. An example is shown.
2/5 ÷ 3/10 = 4/10 ÷ 3/10 = 4/3 = 1 1/3

Method 3: Using a Super Giant One.
To divide by a fraction using a Super Giant One, write the two numbers (dividend and divisor) as a complex fraction with the dividend as the numerator and the divisor as the denominator. Use the reciprocal of the complex fraction’s denominator to create a Super Giant One. Then evaluate as shown in the example.
3/4 ÷ 2/5 = ((3/4)/(2/5)) · ((5/2)/(5/2)) = (3/4 · 5/2)/1 = 3/4 · 5/2 = 15/8 = 1 7/8

Methods & Meanings: MATHEMATICAL PROPERTIES

When two numbers or variables are combined using addition, the order in which they are added does not matter. For example, 7 + 5 = 5 + 7. This fact is known as the Commutative Property of Addition.

Likewise, when two numbers are multiplied together, the order in which they are multiplied does not matter. For example, 5 · 10 = 10 · 5. This fact is known as the Commutative Property of Multiplication.

These results can be generalized using variables: a + b = b + a and a · b = b · a.

Note that subtraction and division do not satisfy the Commutative Property, since 7 − 5 ≠ 5 − 7 and 10 ÷ 5 ≠ 5 ÷ 10.

When three numbers are added, you usually add the first two of them and then add the third one to that result. However, you could also add the last two together and then add the first one to that result. The Associative Property of Addition tells you that the grouping of the numbers does not matter. For example, (7 + 5) + 9 = 7 + (5 + 9).

Likewise, when three numbers are multiplied together, which pair of numbers are multiplied together first does not matter. For example, (5 · (−6)) · 10 is the same as 5 · (−6 · 10). This is the Associative Property of Multiplication.

These results can be generalized using variables: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (a · b) · c = a · (b · c).

Note that subtraction and division do not satisfy the Associative Property, as demonstrated by the following examples:
(7 − 5) − 1 ≠ 7 − (5 − 1)        (10 ÷ 2) ÷ 5 ≠ 10 ÷ (2 ÷ 5)
2 − 1 ≠ 7 − 4                    5 ÷ 5 ≠ 10 ÷ 0.4
1 ≠ 3                            1 ≠ 25

Rearranging the pieces of the rectangle does not change the total area. It does not matter if you think of the area as 8(24), 8(20 + 4), or 8 · 20 + 8 · 4. All of these expressions for the area are equivalent, and they illustrate the Distributive Property of multiplication. An area model can be used to show this multiplication.

The results can be generalized using variables: a(b + c) = a(b) + a(c).

PROPORTIONAL RELATIONSHIPS
A relationship is proportional if one quantity is a multiple of the other. This relationship can be identified in tables, graphs, and equations.
Table: Equivalent ratios of y/x (or x/y) can be seen in a table.
Graph: A straight line through the origin.
Equation: An equation of the form y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.
Example: 3 pounds of chicken costs $7.00. What is the cost for x pounds? Equation: y = 7/3 x
Example: The county fair costs $5.00 to enter and $1.00 per ride. Equation: y = 1x + 5
The relationship between weight and cost is proportional. The table has equivalent ratios (7/3 = 14/6 = 21/9), the graph is a straight line through the origin, and the equation is of the form y = kx.
The relationship between rides and cost is not proportional, because the table does not contain equivalent ratios (6/1 ≠ 7/2 ≠ 8/3), the graph does not pass through the origin, and the equation contains addition.

Methods & Meanings
PART–WHOLE RELATIONSHIPS
Percentages, fractions, and decimals are all different ways to represent a portion of a whole or a number. Portion–whole relationships can also be described in words.
You can represent a part–whole relationship with a double number line model like the one shown. To solve a percentage problem described in words, you must first identify three important quantities: the percent, the whole, and the part of the whole. One of these quantities will be unknown. A diagram can help you organize the information. For example:
There are 220 soccer players in the 8th grade class. If soccer players make up 40% of the 8th graders, how many students are in the whole grade?
Once the parts have been identified, you can use reasoning to extend the part to the whole. For example, if 220 students are 40% of 8th graders, then 10% must be 220 ÷ 4 = 55 students. Another way to solve the problem is to determine the ratio of 220 soccer players to the whole (all students in the grade) and compare that ratio to 40% and 100%. This could be written as 40/100 · ___ = 220/? . Then, 40/100 · 5.5/5.5 = 220/? helps to see that the total number of 8th graders is 550.

Methods & Meanings: CONSECUTIVE INTEGERS

Consecutive integers are integers that come “one after another” in order (that is, without skipping any). For example: 11, 12, and 13 are three consecutive integers. The numbers 10, 12, 14, and 16 are not consecutive integers, but they are consecutive even integers because, in counting up from 10, no even numbers are skipped. Likewise, 15, 17, and 19 are consecutive odd integers.

In algebra, it is sometimes necessary to represent a list of consecutive integers. To represent any list in general, you must use variables. It is common to let n represent the first integer. Here are some examples of how to write a list of consecutive integers.

Three consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
Three consecutive odd integers: n, n + 2, n + 4
Three consecutive even integers: n, n + 2, n + 4

Note that consecutive even integers and odd integers look alike because both even integers and odd integers are two apart. In the list of odd integers, n represents an odd number. In the list of even integers, n represents an even number.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings: ALGEBRA VOCABULARY. Variable: A letter or symbol that represents one or more unknown numbers. Expression: A combination of numbers, variables, and operation symbols. An expression does not contain an equal sign. One example of an expression is 2x + 3(5 − 2x) + 8. In this case, 5 − 2x is a smaller expression within the larger expression. Term: Part of an expression separated from other parts by addition and subtraction. For example, in the expression 2x + 3(5 − 2x) + 8, the three terms are 2x, 3(5 − 2x), and 8. The expression 5 − 2x has two terms, 5 and 2x. Coefficient: The number multiplied by a variable. In the expression 2x + 3(5 − 2x) + 8, 2 is the coefficient of 2x. In the expression 7x − 15x^2, both 7 and 15 are coefficients. Constant term: A number that is not multiplied by a variable. In the expression 2x + 3(5 − 2x) + 8, 8 is a constant term. The number 3 is not a constant term because it is multiplied by a variable inside the parentheses. Factor: Part of a multiplication expression. In the expression 3(5 − 2x), 3 and 5 − 2x are factors.
gpt_oss_or_reasoning: The paragraph only provides definitions of algebraic terms and does not involve any error detection, correction, comparison, or warning about common mistakes.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings: SOLVING INEQUALITIES AND GRAPHING INEQUALITIES ON A NUMBER LINE. An equation always has an equal sign. An inequality has a mathematical inequality (comparison) symbol. To solve an equation or inequality means to determine all the values of the variable that make the comparison true. For example, the solution to x + 3 = 7 is x = 4, and the solution to x − 2 < 5 is x < 7. To solve and graph an inequality with one variable, first treat the problem as if it were an equation and solve for the variable. The solution to the equation is called the boundary point. For example, to solve x − 4 ≥ 8, first solve x − 4 = 8. The solution, x = 12, is the boundary point for the inequality x − 4 ≥ 8. Since the original inequality is true when x = 12, place your boundary point on the number line as a solid point. Then test one value on either side in the original inequality to determine which set of numbers makes the inequality true. This is shown with the examples of x = 8 and x = 15. After testing, you can see that the solution is x ≥ 12. Tip: Test x = 0 as long as x = 0 is not the boundary point. If x = 0 makes the inequality true, shade the region that contains x = 0 up to the boundary point. If x = 0 does not make the inequality true, shade the region that does not contain x = 0 up to the boundary point. When the inequality uses a < or > symbol, the boundary point is not included in the answer. On a number line, this would be indicated with an open circle at the boundary point. For example, the graph of x < 7 is shown.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

CHECKING A SOLUTION

To check a solution to an equation, substitute the solution into the equation and verify that it makes the two sides of the equation equal.

For example, to verify that x = 10 is a solution to the equation 3(x − 5) = 15, substitute 10 into the equation for x and then verify that the two sides of the equation are equal.

As shown, x = 10 is a solution to the equation 3(x − 5) = 15:
x = 10
↓
3(x − 5) = 15
3(10 − 5) = 15
3(5) = 15
15 = 15 (true)

What happens when you do this check if your answer is incorrect? For example, try substituting x = 2 into the same equation. The result shows that x = 2 is not a solution to this equation:
x = 2
↓
3(x − 5) = 15
3(2 − 5) = 15
3(−3) = 15
−9 = 15 (false)
gpt_oss_or_reasoning: The paragraph explains how to check a solution and shows examples of correct and incorrect checks, but does not ask the reader to locate or correct an error, compare students, or warn about common mistakes.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

DEFINING A VARIABLE

When you write an equation, it is important to define the variable precisely. You need to be clear about what you are talking about so that someone else looking at your work would understand what the variable represents. This is an important habit to develop because it is an important step in solving many different math problems.

For example, suppose you have the following problem:
At the neighborhood grocery store, grapes cost $3 a pound. If Belinda spent $5.40 on grapes, how many pounds of grapes did she buy?

One equation you could write is 3x = 5.4 if you know what x stands for. The variable x should be clearly defined, such as x = pounds of grapes, rather than just x = grapes. You could also write g = pounds of grapes, since any letter may be used as a variable.

Methods & Meanings
HISTOGRAMS
A histogram is similar to a bar graph except that each bar represents data in an interval of numbers. The intervals for the data are shown on the horizontal axis. The frequency (number of pieces of data in each interval) is represented by the height of a bar above the interval.

Methods & Meanings
SOLVING PROPORTIONS
An equation stating that two ratios are equal is called a proportion. Some examples of proportions are shown.
6 miles / 2 hours = 9 miles / 3 hours          5/7 = 50/70
Proportions can be used to solve for an unknown part of one ratio where the two ratios are equal. For example, if the ratios 9/2 and x/16 are equal, setting up the proportion x/16 = 9/2 makes it possible for you to solve for x.

USING A GIANT ONE
Since 2 ⋅ 8 = 16, use 8/8 for the Giant One.
9/2 = x/16
9/2 ⋅ [8/8] = x/16
72/16 = x/16
x = 72

UNDOING DIVISION
Think of the ratio x/16 as “x divided by 16.” To solve for x, use the inverse operation of division, which is multiplication. Multiplying both sides of the proportion by 16 “undoes” the division.
x/16 = 9/2
(16/1)(x/16) = (9/2)(16/1)
x = 144/2
x = 72

USING CROSS MULTIPLICATION
This is a solving strategy for proportions that is based on the process of multiplying each side of the equation by the denominators of each ratio and setting the two sides equal. It is a shortcut for using a Fraction Buster (multiplying each side of the equation by the denominators).
FRACTION BUSTER
x/16 = 9/2
2 · 16 · (x/16) = (9/2) · 2 · 16
2 · x = 9 · 16
2x = 144
x = 72
CROSS MULTIPLICATION
x/16 = 9/2
2 · x = 9 · 16
2x = 144
x = 72

9-91. BECOMING MATHEMATICALLY PROFICIENT
During this course, you have been asked lots of different kinds of questions. The purpose of many of the questions is to help you think in new ways.
This course focuses on helping you use some very specific Mathematical Practices. The Mathematical Practices are different ways to approach a mathematics problem, pull it apart, and work on it. They include the ways you communicate mathematics to your teammates and teacher. They are what make you a mathematician, not just a number-cruncher!
Two of the Mathematical Practices you may have used in this activity, for example, are making sense of problems and persevering in solving them and constructing viable arguments and critiquing the reasoning of others. You will learn more about what these mean.
a. With your team, read and discuss the descriptions.
Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them
Making sense of problems and persevering in solving them means that you can solve realistic problems that are full of different kinds of mathematics. These types of problems are not routine, simple, or typical. Instead, they combine lots of mathematical ideas and real-life situations.
In this course, you made sense of such problems and persevered in solving them on a daily basis. You carried out investigations that were not simply “word problems.” By making sense of a problem, rather than being told how to solve it step-by-step, you developed a deeper understanding of mathematics. You also learned how to carry out mathematical procedures fluently and efficiently.
In addition to learning and using problem-solving strategies, you had to stick with challenging problems, trying different strategies and using all of the resources available to you.
Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others
An important practice of mathematics is to construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others. In this course, you regularly shared information, opinions, and expertise with your study team. You took turns talking, listening, contributing, arguing, asking for help, checking for understanding, and keeping each other focused.
During this process, you learned to use higher-order thinking. “Critical thinking” is another way to describe “higher-order thinking.” It can be difficult to learn, but it is extremely valuable. Learning how to think critically helped you understand concepts more deeply. It helped you to apply newfound ideas in all sorts of problems, not just the specific concept you happened to be working on.
You and your study teams used higher-order, critical thinking skills any time you provided clarification, built on each other’s ideas, analyzed a problem by breaking it into smaller parts, came to an agreement during a discussion, and productively criticized each other’s ideas.
Justifying and critiquing was a part of your daily classwork, not an occasional assignment. For each problem, you were expected to communicate your mathematical conclusions in writing, in oral presentations, or in poster presentations in a clear and convincing manner.

UNIT RATE

rate = change in one quantity / change in another quantity
